title: Running a DevSecOps lab for twenty teams

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Imagine twenty student teams all building, testing and deploying software at the same time, in one course. Somebody has to make that run smoothly.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That sounds like running a small tech company.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Nearly. Antoine started as a teaching assistant at Polytechnique Montréal, in the DevSecOps course known as LOG 8100, from September 2024 to January 2026. A good part of his job was behind the scenes.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What did he actually set up?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The course's GitLab workspace: repositories, CI/CD templates, runners and workflows for roughly twenty concurrent teams. Think of it as building a ready-made kitchen, so each team arrives and starts cooking instead of installing the stove.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And in the lab sessions themselves?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: He coached Docker and Kubernetes sessions, covering how to build, deploy and debug, with lab scenarios guided by OWASP security advice. He also refreshed the DevSecOps lab material, graded practicals and coached students through resubmissions.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Why does he say this role matters to him?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Because it's a small platform job. Templates are reusable, runners stay healthy through deadline weeks, and every lab can be reproduced on a student laptop. That's the same discipline he applies to his own CI/CD and homelab, which is why it sits next to his platform engineering experience.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And there was a guest session too, if I remember the photo.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, a guest session with Arctiq in the course. The full post has the photo and links to his other teaching at ETS.
